Fetal Monitoring

Level: Advanced
Topic: Obstetrics / Critical Care Transport
Duration: 60 minutes

Arrival Scenario

You’re transporting a 32-year-old G2P1 at 36 weeks gestation from a rural hospital to a tertiary center. She’s on magnesium for severe preeclampsia. BP 168/102, contracting every 3-4 minutes.

The nurse hands you a fetal monitor strip: “Baseline’s 155, but I’m seeing some decels. Keep an eye on it.”

You look at the strip. The pattern is unmistakable.

And you know exactly what it means.

Warm-Up Questions

Before we interpret strips, answer these:

  1. What’s a normal fetal heart rate range?
  2. What are the three types of decelerations?
  3. What does variability tell you about the fetus?
  4. What’s the difference between early and late decelerations?
  5. When is a fetal heart tracing considered non-reassuring?

Think it through. Fetal monitoring isn’t guessing—it’s pattern recognition.

Explanation / Breakdown

Normal Fetal Heart Rate Parameters

Baseline FHR:

  • Normal: 110-160 bpm
  • Tachycardia: > 160 bpm
  • Bradycardia: < 110 bpm

Variability (Beat-to-Beat Fluctuations):

  • Absent: Amplitude range undetectable
  • Minimal: ≤ 5 bpm amplitude
  • Moderate (Normal): 6-25 bpm amplitude
  • Marked: > 25 bpm amplitude

Why variability matters:
Variability = healthy fetal autonomic nervous system. Moderate variability = reassuring. Absent variability = concerning (fetal distress, hypoxia, or meds).

Accelerations

What they are: Temporary increase in FHR above baseline

Criteria:

  • Peak ≥ 15 bpm above baseline
  • Duration ≥ 15 seconds (but < 2 minutes)
  • < 32 weeks: peak ≥ 10 bpm, duration ≥ 10 seconds

What they mean: REASSURING - indicates fetal well-being

Seen with: Fetal movement, contractions, stimulation

Decelerations

Early Decelerations

Pattern:

  • Gradual decrease (onset to nadir ≥ 30 seconds)
  • Mirrors contraction (starts with contraction, nadir at peak of contraction, returns to baseline as contraction ends)
  • Returns to baseline by end of contraction
  • Usually shallow (rarely < 100 bpm)

Cause: Fetal head compression → vagal response

Significance: BENIGN - normal physiologic response

Management: None needed

Variable Decelerations

Pattern:

  • Abrupt decrease (onset to nadir < 30 seconds)
  • Variable timing relative to contractions (no consistent pattern)
  • Variable depth and duration
  • Rapid return to baseline (usually)
  • Often V-shaped or W-shaped

Cause: Umbilical cord compression

Significance:

  • Mild: Reassuring if brief, moderate variability maintained
  • Moderate/Severe: Concerning if prolonged, deep, or repetitive

Management:

  • Reposition mother (left lateral, right lateral, knee-chest)
  • O2 (non-rebreather)
  • IV fluids
  • Discontinue oxytocin if running
  • Vaginal exam (check for cord prolapse)
  • Notify physician

Late Decelerations

Pattern:

  • Gradual decrease (onset to nadir ≥ 30 seconds)
  • Delayed relative to contraction (nadir occurs AFTER peak of contraction)
  • Slow return to baseline (after contraction ends)
  • Persistent pattern (repetitive)
  • Often subtle (may only drop 10-20 bpm)

Cause: Uteroplacental insufficiency → fetal hypoxia

Significance: OMINOUS - indicates fetal compromise

Management:

  • Reposition mother (left lateral - improve placental perfusion)
  • High-flow O2
  • IV fluid bolus
  • Stop oxytocin
  • Check maternal BP (hypotension worsens placental perfusion)
  • Vaginal exam (rapid labor? abruption?)
  • Prepare for emergency delivery if persistent
  • Notify physician immediately

Prolonged Decelerations

Pattern:

  • Decrease ≥ 15 bpm below baseline
  • Duration ≥ 2 minutes but < 10 minutes
  • Abrupt or gradual

Cause:

  • Cord compression/prolapse
  • Maternal hypotension
  • Uterine hypertonicity
  • Rapid descent
  • Placental abruption
  • Uterine rupture

Significance: CONCERNING - requires immediate evaluation

Management:

  • Reposition
  • O2
  • IV fluids
  • Vaginal exam (cord prolapse?)
  • Stop oxytocin
  • Check maternal status (BP, bleeding, pain)
  • Prepare for emergency delivery if doesn’t resolve

Fetal Heart Rate Categories (NICHD)

Category I (Normal - Reassuring)

  • Baseline 110-160 bpm
  • Moderate variability
  • No late or variable decelerations
  • Accelerations present (not required)
  • Early decelerations present or absent

Action: Routine monitoring

Category II (Indeterminate)

  • Everything that doesn’t fit Category I or III
  • Examples:
    • Minimal or marked variability
    • Tachycardia without variability
    • Variable decelerations with moderate variability
    • Recurrent variable decelerations with minimal/absent variability

Action: Continue monitoring, implement interventions, reassess

Category III (Abnormal - Non-Reassuring)

  • Absent variability AND any of:
    • Recurrent late decelerations
    • Recurrent variable decelerations
    • Bradycardia
  • Sinusoidal pattern

Action: Immediate intervention, prepare for emergent delivery

Causes of FHR Abnormalities

Tachycardia (> 160 bpm):

  • Maternal fever/infection
  • Fetal hypoxia (early sign)
  • Medications (terbutaline, atropine)
  • Fetal arrhythmia
  • Maternal hyperthyroidism
  • Chorioamnionitis

Bradycardia (< 110 bpm):

  • Fetal hypoxia (late sign)
  • Cord compression/prolapse
  • Maternal hypotension
  • Medications (beta-blockers)
  • Fetal heart block
  • Placental abruption

Decreased Variability:

  • Fetal sleep cycle (20-40 min)
  • Fetal hypoxia
  • Medications (magnesium, opioids, sedatives)
  • Prematurity (< 28 weeks)
  • Fetal neurological abnormality

Common Mistakes

Mistake #1: Confusing Early and Late Decelerations

Timing is everything. Early = mirrors contraction. Late = delayed, nadir after peak.

Mistake #2: Ignoring Subtle Late Decelerations

Late decels don’t have to be dramatic. Even small drops (10-15 bpm) are significant if repetitive and late.

Mistake #3: Assuming All Variable Decelerations Are Benign

Mild, brief variables with good variability = okay. Deep, prolonged, repetitive variables = cord compression.

Mistake #4: Not Repositioning the Mother

Left lateral position improves placental perfusion. Always try repositioning first.

Mistake #5: Missing Absent Variability

Flat baseline = concerning (unless explained by sleep cycle or meds). Don’t ignore it.

Mistake #6: Over-Relying on Doppler When Strip Is Available

Continuous monitoring gives you variability and decelerations. Doppler just gives you a number.

Clinical Pearls

💎 Moderate variability is the most reassuring sign. Even with decelerations, if variability is moderate, the fetus is compensating.

💎 Late decelerations = placental insufficiency. Think hypoxia. Act fast.

💎 Variable decelerations = cord compression. Reposition mother. Check for prolapse.

💎 Early decelerations = head compression. Benign. Don’t panic.

💎 Absent variability + recurrent decels = Category III. This baby needs out NOW.

💎 Sinusoidal pattern = severe fetal anemia or hypoxia. Smooth, undulating baseline with no variability. Ominous.

💎 Fetal tachycardia + decreased variability = hypoxia. Don’t wait for bradycardia.

💎 Left lateral position is your first intervention. It improves placental perfusion by relieving aortocaval compression.

💎 O2 helps mom (and therefore baby). 100% O2 via NRB if fetal distress suspected.

💎 Prolonged deceleration > 10 minutes = bradycardia (new baseline). This is bad.

Decision Trees

Fetal Heart Rate Interpretation

Assess Baseline FHR
    ↓
110-160 bpm? (Normal)
    YES → Check Variability
        ↓
        Moderate (6-25 bpm)?
            YES → Check for Decelerations
                ↓
                None or Early Only?
                    → CATEGORY I (Reassuring)
                    → Routine monitoring
                ↓
                Variable Decelerations Present?
                    → Mild/brief with good recovery?
                        YES → CATEGORY II
                        → Continue monitoring
                        → Reposition if needed
                    → Deep/prolonged/repetitive?
                        NO → CATEGORY II-III
                        → Intervene (reposition, O2, fluids)
                ↓
                Late Decelerations Present?
                    → CATEGORY II-III (depending on variability)
                    → Immediate intervention
                    → Prepare for delivery
        ↓
        Minimal/Absent Variability?
            → Check for Decelerations
                ↓
                + Recurrent Late or Variable Decels?
                    → CATEGORY III (Non-Reassuring)
                    → Immediate intervention
                    → Prepare for emergent delivery

    NO → Tachycardia (> 160) or Bradycardia (< 110)?
        → Check Variability
        → Look for cause (fever, hypoxia, meds, cord compression)
        → CATEGORY II or III (depending on variability + decels)

Management of Non-Reassuring Fetal Heart Tracing

Non-Reassuring Pattern Identified
(Late Decels, Severe Variables, Absent Variability + Decels)
    ↓
IMMEDIATE ACTIONS
    ↓
1. Reposition Mother
   - Left lateral (first choice)
   - If no improvement → right lateral or knee-chest

2. Give O2
   - 100% via NRB
   - 10-15 L/min

3. IV Fluid Bolus
   - 500-1000 mL NS or LR
   - Improve maternal BP → improve placental perfusion

4. Stop Oxytocin (if running)
   - Decreased contractions → improved placental perfusion

5. Vaginal Exam
   - Check for cord prolapse
   - Assess cervical dilation (rapid delivery?)

6. Check Maternal Status
   - BP (hypotension?)
   - Bleeding (abruption?)
   - Pain (rupture?)
   - Contractions (hypertonicity?)
    ↓
Reassess Fetal Heart Tracing
    ↓
Improved?
    YES → Continue monitoring closely
    NO → Notify physician/receiving facility
        Prepare for emergent delivery
        Expedite transport

Practice Cases

Case 1: The Late Decelerations

Patient: 28-year-old G1P0 at 39 weeks, laboring
Strip: Baseline 145 bpm, minimal variability, repetitive gradual decelerations starting 20-30 seconds after contraction begins, nadir 10-15 seconds after peak of contraction, slow return to baseline

What’s the pattern and what do you do?

Click for answer **Answer:** Late Decelerations - indicates uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia **Why:** - Gradual decrease (onset to nadir ≥ 30 seconds) - Delayed relative to contraction (nadir AFTER contraction peak) - Repetitive pattern - Minimal variability makes this more concerning **Category:** II-III (depending on persistence) **Action:** 1. **Reposition to left lateral immediately** 2. **100% O2 via NRB** 3. **IV fluid bolus** (500-1000 mL) 4. **Stop oxytocin** (if running) 5. Check maternal BP (hypotension worsens placental perfusion) 6. Notify physician 7. Prepare for potential emergency delivery 8. Continue close monitoring **This is a CONCERNING pattern. Late decelerations indicate the fetus isn't getting enough oxygen during contractions. Intervention is urgent.**

Case 2: The Variable Decelerations

Patient: 32-year-old G3P2 at 38 weeks, active labor
Strip: Baseline 150 bpm, moderate variability, abrupt V-shaped decelerations dropping to 90-100 bpm, occurring at variable times relative to contractions, rapid return to baseline

What’s happening?

Click for answer **Answer:** Variable Decelerations - indicates umbilical cord compression **Why:** - Abrupt decrease (onset to nadir < 30 seconds) - Variable timing (no consistent relationship to contractions) - V-shaped pattern - Rapid recovery - Moderate variability maintained = reassuring **Category:** II (Indeterminate) **Significance:** - Mild to moderate variables with good variability = usually tolerated - Cord compression common in labor (cord wrapped, nuchal cord) - Not immediately dangerous if brief and baby recovers **Action:** 1. **Reposition mother** (left lateral, right lateral, knee-chest) - Changes position of cord 2. **Vaginal exam** (rule out cord prolapse - emergent if present) 3. **O2 if deepening or prolonged** 4. **Continue close monitoring** 5. If worsening (deeper, longer, loss of variability): - IV fluids - Notify physician - Consider amnioinfusion (if available - adds fluid around cord) **Most variable decels resolve with repositioning. Close monitoring is key.**

Case 3: The Flat Line

Patient: 26-year-old G2P1 at 37 weeks, preeclampsia on magnesium sulfate
Strip: Baseline 155 bpm, absent variability (flat baseline), no decelerations, no accelerations

Is this concerning?

Click for answer **Answer:** Yes, concerning - but consider magnesium effect vs. fetal compromise **Why:** - Absent variability = loss of beat-to-beat fluctuations - Can indicate: - Fetal hypoxia (bad) - Fetal sleep cycle (20-40 min - benign) - Magnesium sulfate effect (medication) - Opioid administration (medication) - Prematurity (< 28 weeks) **In this case:** Magnesium sulfate commonly decreases variability **Category:** II (Indeterminate) **Action:** 1. **Check how long variability has been absent** - < 40 minutes + no decels = may be sleep cycle or mag effect - > 40 minutes = more concerning 2. **Stimulate fetus** (if in hospital: vibroacoustic stimulation) 3. **Check magnesium level** (toxicity?) 4. **Monitor closely for decelerations** - Absent variability ALONE = concerning - Absent variability + LATE DECELS = CATEGORY III (emergency) 5. **Notify physician** 6. **Prepare for potential delivery** **Absent variability requires close monitoring. If decelerations develop, this becomes an emergency.**

Case 4: The Prolonged Deceleration

Patient: 35-year-old G4P3 at 40 weeks, rapid labor
Strip: Baseline was 140 bpm with moderate variability, suddenly drops to 80 bpm and stays there for 4 minutes

What’s your immediate action?

Click for answer **Answer:** Prolonged Deceleration - immediate intervention required **Why:** - Deceleration ≥ 15 bpm below baseline - Duration ≥ 2 minutes (but < 10 minutes) - Causes include: - Cord prolapse/compression (check NOW) - Maternal hypotension - Uterine hypertonicity - Rapid descent - Placental abruption - Uterine rupture **This is an EMERGENCY until proven otherwise.** **Action:** 1. **IMMEDIATE vaginal exam** (check for cord prolapse) - If cord palpated: push presenting part up, knee-chest position, emergent delivery 2. **Reposition mother** (left lateral, right lateral, knee-chest) 3. **100% O2** 4. **IV fluid bolus** 5. **Stop oxytocin** (if running) 6. **Check maternal status:** - BP (hypotension?) - Bleeding (abruption?) - Pain (rupture?) 7. **Call for help** 8. **Prepare for emergency delivery** (if doesn't resolve in minutes) **Monitor closely:** - If FHR returns to baseline with moderate variability → continue close monitoring - If remains low or develops absent variability → EMERGENT DELIVERY **Prolonged decelerations are a warning sign. Act fast.**

Case 5: The Sinusoidal Pattern

Patient: 30-year-old G2P1 at 36 weeks, motor vehicle collision 2 hours ago, abdominal pain
Strip: Smooth, undulating sine-wave pattern, baseline 150 bpm, amplitude 5-10 bpm, no variability, no accelerations

What does this pattern indicate?

Click for answer **Answer:** Sinusoidal Pattern - indicates severe fetal anemia or hypoxia (OMINOUS) **Why:** - Sinusoidal = smooth, undulating pattern like a sine wave - Absent true variability - Fixed cycle frequency (3-5 cycles per minute) - Associated with: - **Severe fetal anemia** (most common - Rh isoimmunization, fetomaternal hemorrhage) - Severe fetal hypoxia - Fetal acidosis - In trauma patient with abdominal pain: **think fetomaternal hemorrhage or placental abruption** **Category:** III (Abnormal - Non-Reassuring) **Action:** 1. **Notify physician IMMEDIATELY** 2. **Prepare for EMERGENT DELIVERY** 3. **High-flow O2** 4. **IV access x2, large-bore** 5. **Type and cross** (prepare for transfusion) 6. **Kleihauer-Betke test** (quantify fetomaternal hemorrhage) 7. **Continuous fetal monitoring** 8. **Monitor mother for abruption** (vaginal bleeding, rigid abdomen, shock) 9. **Expedite transport** **This pattern indicates severe fetal compromise. Delivery is often needed urgently.** **Post-trauma patients: sinusoidal pattern + abdominal pain = abruption or fetomaternal hemorrhage until proven otherwise.**

Reflection

Fetal monitoring is about pattern recognition and understanding what the fetus is telling you.

Here’s what you should know:

✅ Normal baseline FHR: 110-160 bpm
✅ Moderate variability is the most reassuring finding
✅ Early decels = benign (head compression)
✅ Variable decels = cord compression (reposition)
✅ Late decels = hypoxia (immediate intervention)
✅ Absent variability + decels = Category III (emergency)
✅ Sinusoidal pattern = severe anemia/hypoxia (ominous)

Next-level thinking:

  • How do you interpret fetal monitoring in preterm labor?
  • What’s the role of fetal scalp stimulation in assessment?
  • When is intrauterine resuscitation appropriate?
  • How does maternal positioning affect placental perfusion?

Your assignment:
Review fetal monitoring strips. Practice identifying baselines, variability, accelerations, and the three types of decelerations. Pattern recognition takes repetition.

Because when you’re transporting a laboring mother, you need to know what that strip is telling you—before it’s too late.
